args.question: What rates of interest have been awarded on motor accident compensation, and from which date does interest run?
args.answer:
Based on the corpus of 56 judgments, the following interest rates and starting dates have been awarded in motor accident compensation cases:

## Interest Rates Awarded

| Rate | Judgment(s) | Court & Year | Key Reasoning |
|------|------------|-------------|--------------|
| **6% p.a.** | **Oriental Insurance Co. vs Soma Devi & Others** (doc_004) | Himachal Pradesh High Court, 2020 | The court noted "a trend of falling interest rates" and that "prevalent interest rates are around 5%", reducing the rate from 7.5% to 6% p.a. |
| **7% p.a.** | **Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Smt. Rani & Ors.** (doc_018) | Allahabad High Court (Lucknow Bench), 2019 | The High Court confirmed the Tribunal's award of 7% p.a., describing it as "the proper rate". |
| **7.5% p.a.** | **Suman Lata vs Madan Mohan Sonkar** (doc_023) | MACT/II Addl. District Judge, Faizabad, 2005 | Reduced from 9% to 7.5%, following the Supreme Court's view in *Tamil Nadu State Road Transport Corp. Ltd. v. Section Raj Priya* that "keeping in view the Bank rate the interest was allowed @ 7.5% per annum only." |
| **9% p.a.** | **Sangeeta Devi vs Mahesh Chand** (doc_022) | MACT Karkardooma Courts, Delhi, 2018 | Awarded 9% p.a. on total compensation from date of filing petition till realization. |
| **9% p.a.** | **No.4 Is A Mother... vs No.1** (doc_041) | IX Addl. Small Causes & MACT, Bangalore, 2016 | Awarded compensation of Rs. 25,95,346/- with interest at 9% p.a. from date of petition. |
| **9% p.a.** | **Raju Gupta vs Himachal Road** (doc_010) | MACT Karkardooma Courts, Delhi, 2018 | Awarded interest @ 9% p.a. on compensation from date of filing petition till realization. |
| **9% p.a.** | **K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun** (doc_034) | MACT Madhugiri, 2001 | Reduced from 12% to 9% p.a., following the Supreme Court in *Kaushnuma Begum v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd.* which held that given the change in economy and RBI policy, 9% is reasonable. |

## Date from Which Interest Runs

In **all cases** where the starting date is specified, interest runs **from the date of filing of the claim petition** (not from the date of accident). The consistent formula used across the corpus is:

> **"Interest @ [X]% p.a. on the total compensation amount from the date of filing of petition till realization."**

This is expressly stated in:
- **doc_004** (Soma Devi): "from the date of filing of the petition, i.e., from 27 Aug 2010"
- **doc_022** (Sangeeta Devi): "from the date of filing of petition till realization"
- **doc_010** (Raju Gupta): "from the date of filing of petition till realization"
- **doc_041** (Mother of deceased): "from the date of the petition till the date of payment"
- **doc_034** (K.G. Srinivasamurthy): "from the date of petition to the date of payment"
- **doc_018** (Smt. Rani): "payable from the date of application till actual payment"

## Summary of Trends

1. **Declining trend over time**: The corpus shows a clear downward trajectory — 12% (reduced to 9% in 2001), then 9% (2005-2018), then 7.5% (2005), then 7% (2011 award, confirmed 2019), and finally 6% (2020). The High Court in *Soma Devi* (2020) explicitly acknowledged falling interest rates as the rationale for 6%.

2. **No single uniform rate**: Courts have discretion. The rate depends on the prevailing economic conditions, bank rates, and the court's assessment of what is "just."

3. **Uniform starting point**: Across all cases, interest runs from the date of filing the claim petition, not the accident date.

supporting.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
supporting.principle: Interest rate on motor accident compensation can be reduced to reflect falling market interest rates; the court reduced it from 7.5% to 6% p.a.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court noted 'prevalent interest rates are around 5%' and reduced the rate accordingly, establishing a precedent for adjusting interest rates to current economic conditions.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most recent High Court authority in the corpus (2020) and reflects the current judicial trend toward lower interest rates.
supporting.quote: The prevalent interest rates are around 5%. As such, it shall be appropriate if the rate of interest on the compensation amount is reduced from 7.5% per annum to 6% per annum, retrospectively, i.e. from the date of the filing of the petition.

supporting.title: The Oriental Insurance Comp. Ltd. ... vs Smt. Rani And Ors.
supporting.principle: Interest at 7% per annum from the date of application till actual payment is a proper rate.
supporting.fact_alignment: The High Court confirmed the Tribunal's award of 7% p.a. as 'the proper rate', providing a mid-range benchmark.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a High Court authority (Allahabad, 2019) that validates 7% as a reasonable rate, sitting between the 6% and 9% extremes.
supporting.quote: The interest is also awarded at the proper rate of 7% per annum, chargeable from the date of petition till the date of actual payment.

supporting.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
supporting.principle: Interest rate on compensation can be reduced from 9% to 7.5% per annum keeping in view prevailing bank rates.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court followed the Supreme Court's view in Tamil Nadu State Road Transport Corp. v. Section Raj Priya that 7.5% is appropriate given bank rates.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a 2005 MACT decision that applied Supreme Court guidance on 7.5% interest, showing the evolution of rates over time.
supporting.quote: keeping in view the Bank rate the interest was allowed @ 7.5% per annum only. In view of the above, we are of the view that the interest should be reduced to 7.5% per annum.

supporting.title: Sangeeta Devi W/O Sh. Vinod Kumar Singh vs Mahesh Chand & Ors
supporting.principle: Interest at 9% p.a. on compensation from the date of filing of petition till realization.
supporting.fact_alignment: A 2018 Delhi MACT decision awarding 9% interest, representing the higher end of the range.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows that some Tribunals continue to award 9% even in the late 2010s, providing a benchmark for claimants seeking higher rates.
supporting.quote: Claimant is also entitled to the interest @ 09% p.a. on the total compensation amount from the date of filing of petition till realization.

supporting.title: No.4 Is A Mother Of The Deceased Sri. M. ... vs No.1
supporting.principle: Interest at 9% p.a. from the date of petition till the date of payment.
supporting.fact_alignment: A 2016 Bangalore MACT decision awarding 9% on a substantial compensation of Rs. 25,95,346/-.
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that 9% was a common rate in the mid-2010s for significant awards.
supporting.quote: The Petitioners are entitled for compensation of Rupees 25,95,346/- with interest at the rate of 9% p.a. from the date of the petition till the date of payment.

supporting.title: Raju Gupta S/O Sh. Madan Mohan Gupta vs Himachal Road
supporting.principle: Interest at 9% p.a. on compensation from the date of filing of petition till realization.
supporting.fact_alignment: A 2018 Delhi MACT decision awarding 9% interest on modest compensation amounts (Rs. 15,000).
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows consistency in the Delhi MACT's approach to 9% interest across different claim sizes.
supporting.quote: Claimant is also entitled to the interest @ 09% p.a. on the total compensation amount from the date of filing of petition till realization.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: Interest rate reduced from 12% to 9% per annum from the date of petition to the date of payment, following the Supreme Court in Kaushnuma Begum.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court applied the Supreme Court's view that given changes in the economy and RBI policy, 9% is reasonable.
supporting.why_it_matters: This 2001 decision shows the historical baseline — Tribunals were awarding 12% before the Supreme Court directed a reduction to 9%.
supporting.quote: The Apex Court in Kaushnuma Begum v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. has held that, in view of the change in the economy and policy of Reserve Bank of India and the prevalent rate of interest for the fixed deposit by the nationalised banks, it would be reasonable to award interest at 9 per cent per annum.

adverse.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
adverse.principle: Interest rates are falling and courts may reduce interest to 6% p.a. to reflect prevailing economic conditions.
adverse.risk_to_client: If a claimant argues for 9% or 12% interest, the insurer can cite this 2020 High Court judgment to argue that 6% is the appropriate current rate given that 'prevalent interest rates are around 5%'. This is the most recent authority in the corpus and directly supports a low interest rate.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This was a Himachal Pradesh High Court decision and may not bind other states. The court was also enhancing compensation under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC while reducing interest — a claimant could argue the interest reduction was a trade-off for the enhancement. Additionally, other Tribunals (Delhi MACT in 2018) continued awarding 9%, showing no uniform rule.
adverse.quote: The prevalent interest rates are around 5%. As such, it shall be appropriate if the rate of interest on the compensation amount is reduced from 7.5% per annum to 6% per annum.

adverse.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
adverse.principle: Interest at 9% can be reduced to 7.5% keeping in view bank rates.
adverse.risk_to_client: If a claimant seeks 9% or higher, the insurer can cite this to argue that even in 2005 the Supreme Court-approved rate was 7.5%, and rates have only fallen since then.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a 2005 MACT decision, not a High Court or Supreme Court precedent on the point. The bank rates in 2005 were different from current rates. Claimants can argue that 9% has continued to be awarded by other Tribunals (doc_022, doc_010) even after this decision.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: Interest at 12% is excessive and should be reduced to 9% following Supreme Court guidance.
adverse.risk_to_client: If a claimant argues for interest above 9%, the insurer can cite this to show that even in 2001 the Supreme Court capped interest at 9%, and rates have only declined since then.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a 2001 decision that actually supports 9% — which is the rate many claimants seek. It only hurts a claimant seeking more than 9%. The economic context has changed significantly since 2001.

priority_arguments: Interest runs from the date of filing the claim petition, not the date of the accident — this is uniform across all judgments in the corpus.

The prevailing rate has declined over time: 12% (pre-2001) → 9% (2001-2018) → 7.5% (2005) → 7% (2011/2019) → 6% (2020). A claimant should argue for 9% based on the multiple MACT decisions in 2016-2018 that awarded this rate.
If arguing for the claimant: cite doc_022, doc_041, and doc_010 (all awarding 9% as late as 2016-2018) to show that 9% remains a legitimate rate.
If arguing for the insurer: cite doc_004 (2020 High Court reducing to 6%) as the most recent and highest-authority decision, reflecting current economic reality.
The starting date is uniformly 'from the date of filing of the petition' — no judgment in the corpus awards interest from the accident date.
strategy.compensation_range: 6% to 9% per annum, depending on the court, year of decision, and prevailing economic conditions.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The corpus shows a clear downward trajectory. The most recent High Court authority (doc_004, 2020) reduced interest to 6%. However, MACTs in Delhi continued awarding 9% as late as 2018 (doc_022, doc_010). The Allahabad High Court in 2019 confirmed 7% as proper (doc_018). The range reflects judicial discretion based on bank rates and economic conditions.
risks: The 2020 Himachal Pradesh High Court decision (doc_004) reducing interest to 6% is the most recent and highest-authority judgment in the corpus on this point — it may be followed by other courts.
There is no Supreme Court decision in this corpus that prescribes a uniform interest rate for motor accident compensation; the rate is at the court's discretion.
If arguing for a higher rate (9%), the opposing side will point to the declining trend and the 2020 6% decision as reflecting current economic reality.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: For a claimant: argue for 9% p.a. from date of petition, citing the consistent line of MACT decisions (doc_022, doc_041, doc_010). For an insurer: argue for 6% p.a. citing doc_004, or at most 7% citing doc_018.

caveats: This corpus contains only 56 judgments, of which only 7 specifically address interest rates. The sample is limited and may not reflect the full range of judicial practice.
No Supreme Court judgment in this corpus directly prescribes a uniform interest rate for motor accident compensation. The rates are set at the discretion of individual courts and Tribunals.

The corpus is mixed — it includes judgments from different states (Himachal Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Delhi, Karnataka) and different court levels (MACT and High Court), so the rates may vary by jurisdiction.
doc_018 (Smt. Rani) confirmed 7% but the original Tribunal award was from 2011, confirmed in 2019 — the rate may reflect the 2011 economic context rather than current conditions.

result.question: What rates of interest have been awarded on motor accident compensation, and from which date does interest run?

supporting.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
supporting.principle: Interest rate on motor accident compensation can be reduced to reflect falling market interest rates; the court reduced it from 7.5% to 6% p.a.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court noted 'prevalent interest rates are around 5%' and reduced the rate accordingly, establishing a precedent for adjusting interest rates to current economic conditions.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most recent High Court authority in the corpus (2020) and reflects the current judicial trend toward lower interest rates.
supporting.quote: The prevalent interest rates are around 5%. As such, it shall be appropriate if the rate of interest on the compensation amount is reduced from 7.5% per annum to 6% per annum, retrospectively, i.e. from the date of the filing of the petition.

supporting.title: The Oriental Insurance Comp. Ltd. ... vs Smt. Rani And Ors.
supporting.principle: Interest at 7% per annum from the date of application till actual payment is a proper rate.
supporting.fact_alignment: The High Court confirmed the Tribunal's award of 7% p.a. as 'the proper rate', providing a mid-range benchmark.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a High Court authority (Allahabad, 2019) that validates 7% as a reasonable rate, sitting between the 6% and 9% extremes.
supporting.quote: The interest is also awarded at the proper rate of 7% per annum, chargeable from the date of petition till the date of actual payment.

supporting.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
supporting.principle: Interest rate on compensation can be reduced from 9% to 7.5% per annum keeping in view prevailing bank rates.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court followed the Supreme Court's view in Tamil Nadu State Road Transport Corp. v. Section Raj Priya that 7.5% is appropriate given bank rates.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a 2005 MACT decision that applied Supreme Court guidance on 7.5% interest, showing the evolution of rates over time.
supporting.quote: keeping in view the Bank rate the interest was allowed @ 7.5% per annum only. In view of the above, we are of the view that the interest should be reduced to 7.5% per annum.

supporting.title: Sangeeta Devi W/O Sh. Vinod Kumar Singh vs Mahesh Chand & Ors
supporting.principle: Interest at 9% p.a. on compensation from the date of filing of petition till realization.
supporting.fact_alignment: A 2018 Delhi MACT decision awarding 9% interest, representing the higher end of the range.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows that some Tribunals continue to award 9% even in the late 2010s, providing a benchmark for claimants seeking higher rates.
supporting.quote: Claimant is also entitled to the interest @ 09% p.a. on the total compensation amount from the date of filing of petition till realization.

supporting.title: No.4 Is A Mother Of The Deceased Sri. M. ... vs No.1
supporting.principle: Interest at 9% p.a. from the date of petition till the date of payment.
supporting.fact_alignment: A 2016 Bangalore MACT decision awarding 9% on a substantial compensation of Rs. 25,95,346/-.
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that 9% was a common rate in the mid-2010s for significant awards.
supporting.quote: The Petitioners are entitled for compensation of Rupees 25,95,346/- with interest at the rate of 9% p.a. from the date of the petition till the date of payment.

supporting.title: Raju Gupta S/O Sh. Madan Mohan Gupta vs Himachal Road
supporting.principle: Interest at 9% p.a. on compensation from the date of filing of petition till realization.
supporting.fact_alignment: A 2018 Delhi MACT decision awarding 9% interest on modest compensation amounts (Rs. 15,000).
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows consistency in the Delhi MACT's approach to 9% interest across different claim sizes.
supporting.quote: Claimant is also entitled to the interest @ 09% p.a. on the total compensation amount from the date of filing of petition till realization.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: Interest rate reduced from 12% to 9% per annum from the date of petition to the date of payment, following the Supreme Court in Kaushnuma Begum.
supporting.fact_alignment: The court applied the Supreme Court's view that given changes in the economy and RBI policy, 9% is reasonable.
supporting.why_it_matters: This 2001 decision shows the historical baseline — Tribunals were awarding 12% before the Supreme Court directed a reduction to 9%.
supporting.quote: The Apex Court in Kaushnuma Begum v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. has held that, in view of the change in the economy and policy of Reserve Bank of India and the prevalent rate of interest for the fixed deposit by the nationalised banks, it would be reasonable to award interest at 9 per cent per annum.

adverse.title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi & Others
adverse.principle: Interest rates are falling and courts may reduce interest to 6% p.a. to reflect prevailing economic conditions.
adverse.risk_to_client: If a claimant argues for 9% or 12% interest, the insurer can cite this 2020 High Court judgment to argue that 6% is the appropriate current rate given that 'prevalent interest rates are around 5%'. This is the most recent High Court authority in the corpus and directly supports a low interest rate.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This was a Himachal Pradesh High Court decision and may not bind other states. The court was also enhancing compensation under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC while reducing interest — a claimant could argue the interest reduction was a trade-off for the enhancement. Additionally, other Tribunals (Delhi MACT in 2018) continued awarding 9%, showing no uniform rule.
adverse.quote: The prevalent interest rates are around 5%. As such, it shall be appropriate if the rate of interest on the compensation amount is reduced from 7.5% per annum to 6% per annum.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Interest at more than 6% cannot be awarded in MACT claims because Section 34 CPC governs interest on judgments in the absence of a specific provision in the MV Act.
adverse.risk_to_client: This 2024 Bangalore MACT decision, citing the Karnataka High Court in Vijay Ishwar Jadhav, holds that Section 34 CPC caps interest and 'interest at the rate of more than 6% could not have been awarded.' This directly undermines any claim for 9% interest and provides a legal argument — not just a factual one about falling rates — that 6% is the ceiling.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a single MACT decision, not a binding precedent outside Karnataka. The reasoning that Section 34 CPC governs MACT interest is debatable — Section 169 of the MV Act makes CPC applicable only to the extent of procedure, and Section 149(1) of the MV Act itself contemplates interest. Other courts (Delhi MACT, Allahabad High Court) have awarded 7-9% without applying a Section 34 CPC cap.
adverse.quote: the provisions of Section 34 of C.P.C., 1908. Thus, in the given circumstances of this case, interest at the rate of more than 6% could not have been awarded.
